title: Did the Black Death reach sub-Saharan Africa in the fourteenth century?
short: Plague devastated Egypt and North Africa in 1347–49, but whether it crossed the Sahara or reached the Horn and East Africa is unresolved.
matters: If plague reached West, East or Northeast Africa, it would offer an explanation for site abandonments, settlement shifts and political reorganizations that archaeologists date to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, from the forest zone of southern Ghana to Ife, and it would change how historians read the demographic and political background to the Atlantic encounter. It also bears on the global history of the second pandemic, on whether the Yersinia pestis lineages now endemic in Central and East Africa descend from medieval introductions, and on the long-standing assumption that Africa south of the Sahara was untouched while Eurasia and North Africa lost a large share of their populations.
stuck: Written sources from sub-Saharan Africa for the fourteenth century are few, and Arabic chroniclers who described plague in Egypt and the Maghrib were largely silent about lands beyond the Sahara, a silence that can be read either as absence of plague or absence of reporting. Archaeological signs such as abandonments, mass burials or population decline have other possible causes (drought, war, trade shifts), and few sites are dated precisely enough to tie them to the 1340s–1400s. No medieval Y. pestis genome has yet been published from sub-Saharan Africa, so the genetic argument rests on inferences from the phylogeny of modern African strains.
solved: Recovery of Yersinia pestis DNA, radiocarbon-dated to c. 1340–1500, from human remains at one or more sub-Saharan sites, placed on the second-pandemic phylogeny; or, conversely, systematic negative screening of well-dated fourteenth- and fifteenth-century burials across several regions combined with a full survey of the textual evidence showing no plague references.
approach: Start from the regional work already done: Chouin (2018) on the fourteenth-century abandonment of earthwork settlements in southern Ghana and at Ife, Gallagher (2018) on which archaeological signatures can and cannot distinguish plague from drought or war, Derat (2018) on Ge'ez lexical and talismanic evidence from the Horn, and Green (2018) on what the phylogeny of modern African strains does and does not show. Chapelain de Seréville-Niel (2022) and Chapelain de Seréville-Niel (2024) set out what the already excavated skeletal material from Benin City and Ile-Ife can bear, including a mass grave opened in the early 1960s.

Build from the archaeological literature a geo-referenced register of candidate sites and of human remains, with radiocarbon determinations recorded as calibrated ranges and with the original laboratory codes. The choice that shapes everything after it is whether a candidate is defined by settlement disruption or by dated human remains whose range overlaps c. 1340-1500; these are different classes of evidence and should be kept separate rather than merged into one map of 'plague sites'.

In parallel, compile a dated register of references to epidemic mortality, and of the places and years for which sources are silent, from Arabic and Ge'ez texts, fifteenth-century Portuguese accounts in the Torre do Tombo, and the West African manuscripts imaged from Timbuktu and the Ethiopian collections in the Endangered Archives Programme. Most of these manuscripts are later copies, so each reference needs its witness dated by specialists before it counts as fourteenth-century testimony.

Some progress needs no new excavation: re-screening the published shotgun data from African ancient-DNA studies held in the European Nucleotide Archive, including the medieval Swahili coast individuals sequenced by Brielle (2023), with authentication workflows such as the one described by Pochon (2023), and reporting coverage and detection limits for each individual. Even a set of negatives establishes how many dated burials have now been tested and how deeply.

The two hypotheses can be stated so that evidence separates them. Chouin (2018) and Green (2020) argue for fourteenth-century introductions south of the Sahara, while Mas Fiol (2024), working from a large collection of modern isolates, dates the spread of the 1.ANT lineage into continental Africa to the late seventeenth century and after; a medieval genome from a sub-Saharan burial, placed on the second-pandemic framework of Spyrou (2019), would decide between them, and its absence would not. Until then the honest output is region by region, plague attested, screened without detection, or untested, rather than a single continental verdict.

Everything beyond the computational re-screening depends on institutions: ancient-DNA laboratories, and museums and heritage authorities in Nigeria, Ghana, Tanzania and Ethiopia, which hold both the remains and the excavation records, among them the Kilwa Kisiwani and Aksum field archives of the British Institute in Eastern Africa. Sampling and radiocarbon dating should proceed under protocols agreed with those authorities and with descendant communities, and with African archaeologists and bioarchaeologists reviewing both the registers and any laboratory result.

existing.authors: Gérard L. Chouin and Christopher R. DeCorse
existing.title: Prelude to the Atlantic Trade: New Perspectives on Southern Ghana's Pre-Atlantic History (800–1500)
existing.note: Dated the abandonment of earthwork-enclosed settlements in southern Ghana to the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries and raised epidemic disease as a possible cause.

existing.title: Yersinia pestis Genome Sequencing Identifies Patterns of Global Phylogenetic Diversity
existing.note: Global phylogeny of modern Y. pestis that placed African Antiqua (1.ANT) strains on a branch arising shortly after the medieval polytomy, later used by historians to argue for a medieval introduction to Africa.

existing.title: A Draft Genome of Yersinia pestis from Victims of the Black Death
existing.note: First reconstructed Black Death genome (London, 1348–50), establishing the method that could be applied to African remains.

existing.title: Taking 'Pandemic' Seriously: Making the Black Death Global
existing.venue: The Medieval Globe 1: Pandemic Disease in the Medieval World: Rethinking the Black Death
existing.note: Argued that genetics required historians to consider regions, including sub-Saharan Africa, absent from the traditional Black Death narrative.

existing.title: Reflections on Plague in African History (14th–19th c.)
existing.note: Develops the hypothesis that plague reached West Africa in the fourteenth century, drawing on site abandonments in the forest zone, including southern Ghana and Ife, and on discontinuities in oral tradition.

existing.title: Putting Africa on the Black Death Map: Narratives from Genetics and History
existing.note: Reads the phylogeny of modern African Y. pestis strains as evidence for medieval introductions and outlines what aDNA testing would need to show.

existing.authors: Daphne E. Gallagher and Stephen A. Dueppen
existing.title: Recognizing Plague Epidemics in the Archaeological Record of West Africa
existing.note: Assesses which archaeological signatures could and could not distinguish plague from other causes of disruption in West African sites.

existing.title: Du lexique aux talismans: occurrences de la peste dans la Corne de l'Afrique du XIIIe au XVe siècle
existing.note: Identifies Ge'ez terms, hagiographic episodes and protective texts that may refer to plague in medieval Ethiopia.

existing.title: Phylogeography of the Second Plague Pandemic Revealed through Analysis of Historical Yersinia pestis Genomes
existing.note: Traced the diversification of second-pandemic strains across Europe and western Eurasia from medieval genomes, a framework into which any African genome would be placed.

existing.title: A Fistful of Shells: West Africa from the Rise of the Slave Trade to the Age of Revolution
existing.note: Synthesis of West African history that engages the possibility of fourteenth-century epidemic disruption as background to Atlantic contact.

existing.title: The Four Black Deaths
existing.note: Reframes the Black Death as a series of thirteenth- and fourteenth-century strain radiations, including routes toward Africa.

existing.title: The Source of the Black Death in Fourteenth-Century Central Eurasia
existing.note: Located the second pandemic's ancestral strain in the Tian Shan c. 1338, fixing the starting point from which any spread to Africa must be measured.

existing.authors: Cécile Chapelain de Seréville-Niel and Gérard Chouin
existing.title: Témoins africains de crises sanitaires ?
existing.note: Reassesses human remains excavated at Benin City and Ile-Ife since the 1960s, including a mass grave, for signs of a medieval health crisis.

existing.title: Entwined African and Asian Genetic Roots of Medieval Peoples of the Swahili Coast
existing.note: Human aDNA from medieval and early modern Swahili coast burials, showing that suitable dated remains and sequencing data already exist for pathogen screening.

existing.title: aMeta: An Accurate and Memory-Efficient Ancient Metagenomic Profiling Workflow
existing.note: Open workflow for detecting and authenticating microbial DNA in ancient shotgun data, of the kind needed to re-screen published African sequencing data for Y. pestis.

existing.authors: Cécile Chapelain de Seréville-Niel, Gérard Chouin and Adisa Ogunfolakan
existing.title: Retour sur l'archéologie funéraire médiévale du Sud-Ouest du Nigeria
existing.note: Examines the stratigraphy, body positions and bone markings of the Benin City and Ile-Ife remains against both the plague hypothesis and pre-Atlantic mortuary practice.

existing.title: Global Evolutionary Patterns of Yersinia pestis and Its Spread into Africa
existing.note: Sequenced over a thousand modern isolates from the Institut Pasteur collection and dated the spread of the 1.ANT lineage into continental Africa to the late seventeenth century onward, against a medieval introduction; preprint, not yet peer reviewed.

archives.repository: Hill Museum & Manuscript Library (vHMML Reading Room), Collegeville, Minnesota
archives.collection: Digitized Timbuktu and Malian manuscript collections (SAVAMA-DCI and private libraries)
archives.note: Imaged Arabic and Ajami manuscripts from Mali, mostly later than the fourteenth century but including chronicles and medical texts that may record earlier epidemics; free registration.

holdings.name: Aboubacar Ben Said Library (SAVAMA-DCI project)
holdings.note: Private Timbuktu family library of about 7,000 items, with 7,563 digital surrogates catalogued in the Reading Room.

holdings.name: Mamma Haidara Library (SAVAMA-DCI project)
holdings.note: Family library of SAVAMA's founder, Abdel Kader Haidara, digitized by HMML and partly available in the Reading Room.

archives.repository: British Library, Endangered Archives Programme, London
archives.collection: Ethiopian monastic and church manuscript surveys (Ge'ez hagiographies, chronicles and magical-protective texts)
archives.note: Open-access images of Ethiopian manuscript collections relevant to Derat's lexical and talismanic evidence for plague.

holdings.name: EAP286: Institute of Ethiopian Studies manuscript digitization, Addis Ababa
holdings.note: General collection of imaged Ethiopian manuscripts, mainly Ge'ez, with Amharic, Arabic, Harari and Oromo items; access is for research purposes only.

archives.repository: British Institute in Eastern Africa, Nairobi
archives.collection: Archaeological archive, including Neville Chittick's excavation records for Kilwa Kisiwani, Aksum and Mogadishu (1961–1983)
archives.note: Field notes, plans and photographs from Swahili coast and Horn excavations, partly digitized via the Archaeology Data Service; access by appointment.

holdings.name: BIEA Digital Archives: Kilwa Kisiwani
holdings.note: Images and slides from Neville Chittick's excavations at Kilwa Kisiwani, Tanzania, hosted by the Archaeology Data Service.

holdings.name: BIEA Digital Archives: Aksum
holdings.note: Images and documents from excavations at Aksum, Ethiopia, hosted by the Archaeology Data Service.

archives.collection: Raw sequencing data from published ancient DNA studies of African individuals (e.g. Swahili coast, Nubia, Ethiopia)
archives.note: Public shotgun data from existing aDNA studies that can be re-screened computationally for Y. pestis reads before new sampling.

archives.repository: Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo, Lisbon
archives.collection: Corpo Cronológico and chancery records for fifteenth-century Portuguese voyages to West Africa
archives.note: Earliest European eyewitness accounts of the West African coast, useful for testing claims of depopulation in the century after 1350.
